newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean businessmen unimpressed by NAFTA talk.
newsitem.headline: Chilean businessmen unimpressed by NAFTA talk.

text.p: Chilean businessmen, jaded by years of talk but no action on joining NAFTA, reacted with weary scepticism on Thursday to President Bill Clinton's pledge to push for Chile's inclusion in the pact.

Clinton called on Congress on Thursday to give him "fast track" negotiating authority to allow him to revive talks on Chile's entry to the North American trade bloc that stalled a year ago due to differences with the Republicans.

"What matters to us is that this declaration of intent becomes a reality, although this issue is not something we... will lose much sleep over," said Carlos Astudillo, manager of the Mechanical and Metallurgical Industrialists Association.

Astudillo's reaction reflected the disenchantment among businessmen at the lack of progress in the talks to join the North American Free Trade Agreement joining the United States, Canada and Mexico. Talks began in December 1994 but have gone nowhere because of the lack of fast-track.
In the meantime, Chile has signed a free trade accord with Canada and the four-nation Mercosur trade bloc. It also plans to sign a free trade deal with the European Union.

Chilean manufacturers were sceptical that membership of the NAFTA would boost their exports, saying that the recent rise in the dollar against the Chilean peso and not tariffs were their greatest concern.
"First we must be worried about being competitive more than signing agreements," said Roberto Fantuzzi, president of the Manufacturing Exporters Association.
"Most of Chile's manufacturing sector...already has zero tariffs. The real problem is that the exchange rate is not going to allow us to export."
Clinton assured President Eduardo Frei personally of his support for Chile's push to join NAFTA in talks at the White House on Wednesday.
Chile was invited to join NAFTA at the Summit of the Americas in Miami in December 1994. But it has refused to enter binding talks unless U.S. officials have "fast-track" negotiating authority.
The authority would allow U.S. trade representatives to cut an accord with Chile without fear that it would later be changed by Congress under pressure from special interest groups.
"We really need to pass the fast-track authority, we need to do it this year and we need to do it as soon as possible," Clinton said in a speech in Washington.
Clinton faces big problems in getting Congress to pass "fast-track" authority, with Democratic legislators saying it would be a mistake to extend NAFTA in its existing form.
Frei ends a four-day visit to the United States on Friday.
